input.brief: Online tribute pages: you upload photos, a message and a timeline for someone you love, preview it free, pay once to publish and send them the link as a gift

direction.name: The page is the object
direction.idea: Find the printed or physical artefact that already exists in the subject's world and build the page as that thing. A wedding site is the invitation card. A restaurant is its menu. A conference is the ticket; a record is its sleeve; a shop is the receipt or the swing tag; an archive is a stack of tabbed folders; a course is the syllabus sheet. The artefact supplies everything a template would otherwise invent: its proportions, its typographic manners, its way of grouping information. Visitors recognise the object instantly, which is why these pages feel specific.
direction.composition: The first screen shows the artefact as a single filled panel (paper colour on a contrasting ground) centred or offset, with believable proportions: a card at 5:7, a ticket at about 2.2:1 with a notch cut by `clip-path`, a menu as a tall sheet. All primary content lives on it, set the way that object is set: centred and symmetrical for an invitation, in tidy aligned columns for a menu or ticket. The ground behind is a flat colour or one full-bleed photograph. As the page continues, each section is another piece of the same stationery: a second card, a tear-off stub, a folded panel, always filled shapes with real edges (straight, notched, scalloped, perforated by a dotted `border` of round dots at 4px or more), never outlined boxes. The footer is the back of the object.
direction.typography: Take the manners of the artefact: a bookish serif with small caps avoided, or a blunt condensed face for tickets and posters. Sizes stay within what print would use relative to the panel; the name is large on the panel, details are small and exact.
direction.colour: Paper and ink plus the ground the paper sits on. Two or three flat colours in total, like a two-colour print job.
direction.imagery: Optional. One photograph behind the object, or small photographs placed on it like tipped-in plates. The object itself is the image.
direction.richness: Recognition. The shaped edges, the print-like alignment and the limited inks make a familiar object out of plain HTML.
direction.pitfalls: Choose an artefact that truly belongs to the subject, or it becomes costume. Shape the edges with fills and `clip-path`; an outlined rectangle with a thin border is not an object. Keep text sizes readable on a phone, where the object becomes full width with its shaped edge kept at top and bottom.

hero.name: Striped card beside the room
hero.blueprint: The viewport is split 50/50 with a 12px gap and 12px outer margins. The right half is one full-height photograph of the room, corners radiused 16px, `position: sticky` so it stays in view while the left half scrolls. The left half is a printed card: a flat paper-colour panel with the same 16px radius, and the subject's stripe (from its awning, label or ribbon) as the only ornament. Across the card's top runs a band 56px tall made of alternating bars of the single ink colour and paper, each bar 28px wide, built as a flex row of filled blocks. The same stripe returns as an 8px band above the footer and inside the button on hover. Under the band, centred: the wordmark about 300px wide, then a two-line headline in a light serif at clamp(40px, 3.6vw, 56px) in the ink colour, one supporting sentence at 17px held to 36ch, and the single action as a solid rectangular button. Three text links sit in one centred row at 15px, 28px above the card's bottom edge. One ink on paper; the photograph supplies every other colour.
hero.mobile: The photograph comes first at full width inside 12px margins, 48svh tall, with the 16px radius. The card follows and overlaps the photograph's bottom edge by 24px using a negative margin. Its striped band is 40px tall; below it the wordmark at 56% width, the headline at 8vw on two lines, the sentence and the button, all centred. The links wrap into the card's foot.
hero.headline: A warm two-line welcome of three to six words, up to about 18 characters per line at 3.6vw.

type.note: One neo-grotesk doing everything: semibold headings pulled tight, small regular text, no capitals and no second voice. Suits software, hardware and studio pages that want to look exact and unshowy.

palette.name: Oxblood and grey
palette.note: Deep red text on grey paper holds most of the page, then pale grey text on a solid red field takes one long section and the footer. Photographs are desaturated so nothing breaks the pair, and the button is a solid red block.

motion.name: Slow crossfade
motion.description: The principal photograph quietly changes: three or four images of the same framing crossfade over about 1.6 seconds, holding five to six seconds each, or the fixed image changes when its matching section arrives. It should feel like light shifting in a room. Pause when the tab is hidden; under reduced motion show only the first image.

sections.name: Square plate, spare text
sections.blueprint: One flat field split 50/50, at least 88svh tall. Left half: a single square photograph filling the half's width minus 40px margins, vertically centred, square corners. A large simple shape may be laid over it to turn the photograph into the object it stands for: a ring 86% of its width with a 6px stroke and a small solid dot at the centre makes a record; a notch cut by clip-path makes a ticket stub. Right half, a flex column with space-between: at the top a row of three plain text tabs at 18px (editions, years, variants), the active one in full ink and the others at 40%; in the middle the title, two to four words at 32–40px bold, with a 34ch description 48px below; along the bottom two filled rectangular cells side by side, each half the column wide and 72px tall, acting as the two actions, one in ink and one a tone off the field.
sections.mobile: The square photograph comes first at full width with 16px margins. The tabs sit under it as one row at 17px. Then the title at 28px, the description, and the two action cells stacked, each full width and 60px tall.

sections.name: Itinerary on a slip
sections.blueprint: The process is printed as an itinerary or receipt. One paper-coloured slip 420–480px wide stands on a contrasting flat ground at columns 7–11; its bottom edge is a zigzag cut with clip-path and its top edge is straight. The heading, two to four words at clamp(40px, 4.4vw, 68px), sits in columns 1–5 with a 30ch paragraph, top-aligned with the slip. On the slip, in the text face at 16px with tabular figures: stages grouped under time headings that carry the order ('Monday', 'Midweek', 'Friday'), each heading in bold with 28px above it. Under a heading, two to four rows; each row has what happens on the left, a duration or time on the right, and a leader of round 4px dots between. The final row is inverted, paper-coloured text on a full-width ink bar 44px tall, and states the result: what the reader holds at the end and the total time.
sections.mobile: The heading and paragraph come first. The slip follows at full width minus 16px margins, keeping its zigzag bottom edge. Rows keep left text, dots and right value on one line; long descriptions wrap under the left text. The inverted final row stays full width.

sections.name: Photo tiles with label strips
sections.blueprint: Four columns with 12px gaps; every tile is a photograph with a filled label strip attached directly beneath it, the two forming one object like a print with its swing tag. The photograph is 1:1 or 4:5 with square corners. The strip is the same width, 84–96px tall with 12px padding, and holds two or three rows of text at 12–13px in the text face with tabular figures: row one spreads four short values evenly across the width with `justify-content: space-between`; row two puts a date at the left end and a time or place at the right end; row three names the maker or model. Strip and text colours change per tile through four palette pairs (dark on bright, bright on dark), so a uniform grid looks varied. Rows of tiles are 28px apart. A two- or three-word heading at 32px sits top-left, 40px above the grid. Holds 8–16 tiles.
sections.mobile: Two columns with 8px gaps. Strips keep two rows only: the four values wrap to two per row, and the date and place line is dropped. Text stays at 12px. The heading sits above at 24px. Colour pairs keep rotating so adjacent tiles never match.

sections.name: Prices like a menu
sections.blueprint: Prices set the way a good menu sets them. A heading of two to three words at 32–40px sits in columns 1–3. Columns 5–12 hold the list in two text columns with a 64px gap. Items are grouped under plain group names at 24px in medium weight with 48px above each group. Each item is a row: the name at 19px on the left, the price at the same size on the right on the same baseline, with tabular figures and the currency sign shown only once per group; beneath the name, one line of description at 16px in the softer ink, no wider than 36ch. Rows are 22px apart. Name and price are joined only by empty space (flex with `justify-content: space-between`), with no dot leaders and no lines. One small photograph (4:5, three columns wide) may sit under the heading in the left zone.
sections.mobile: One column. The heading at 28px, then the photograph at 60% width if used. Each item keeps name left and price right on one line at 17px, with its description beneath in the softer ink. Group names at 20px with 40px above.

sections.name: Answers as reading text
sections.blueprint: The questions and answers are set as continuous reading text, like the notes at the back of a programme. A heading of two or three words at 28–32px sits in columns 1–3, top-aligned. Columns 5–12 hold the text in two columns (`columns: 2; column-gap: 56px`), each about 36ch wide, at 16–17px with leading 1.55. Each item is one paragraph: the question is the opening run-in, set in the medium weight in the full ink and ending with its question mark, and the answer continues on the same line in the regular weight. Paragraphs are separated by 20px and carry `break-inside: avoid` so none splits across columns. No toggles, no icons, no boxes. Eight to fourteen items fit on one screen, which is the point: everything is answered at a glance. Where the page's reading column is narrow, use one column.
sections.mobile: One column at 16px with 20px margins. The heading leads at 24px. Each paragraph keeps its run-in question in the medium weight, with 18px between paragraphs. The section may run to two screens; do not collapse it into an accordion.

sections.name: A sentence with a blank
sections.blueprint: The closing sentence has a gap in it, and the gap is the form. A sentence of five to eight words is set at about 6vw on two lines, flush left across columns 1–11; there is no separate heading. Where the reader's email (or name, or city) belongs, an `<input>` sits inline on the baseline: a filled block of the one-step tone, exactly one line-height tall and about 7em wide, with the placeholder in the same face and size in the softer ink, no border, and the page's radius or motif corner. The sentence's last word is the submit `<button>`, set in the same type on a block of the accent colour of the same height. Field and button use `em` units so they scale with the sentence. One line at 16px under the sentence, in the softer ink, says what happens after sending. Nothing else is in the section.
sections.mobile: The sentence is set at 10vw on two lines; the input drops to a line of its own between them at full width and one line-height tall, and the final word, as the button, ends the second line. The explaining line follows at 15px.

sections.name: The mark, built large
sections.blueprint: On a flat colour field, the brand closes the page as a construction rather than as set type. Across the full content width and about 34svh tall, the wordmark is built from blocks: each letter is knocked out of its own solid rectangle in a palette colour, the rectangles differ in height (60–100% of the band) and butt together with 4px gaps, bottoms on one line. Where the project has a simple geometric mark or motif, enlarge that instead, drawn as inline SVG from flat rectangles, circles and quarter-arcs with the same 4px gaps. Below, 56px lower: four columns of plain links at 15px across columns 1–8, and two addresses or contact lines in columns 9–12. A last row carries the copyright at the left and one small filled button at the right. Space and the block construction do all the separating.
sections.mobile: The block wordmark spans the full width at about 22svh tall; a long name breaks into two rows of blocks. Link columns go two across at 15px, contact lines beneath at full width, then copyright and the small button on one row.

references.name: WeekSync
references.idea: The page is a paper coupon: a dotted cut line with a scissors icon frames the viewport, and on scroll the navigation rail is cut free while the rest of the sheet tilts and falls away.
references.hero: Taupe-grey field wrapped by a black dotted rounded-rectangle border inset 16px from every edge. A left rail about 26% wide holds, centred on its own axis, a small black logo glyph at the top, a two-line mono tagline and a text link in braces; four nav labels, each under a small empty circle, stack at the bottom of the rail. A scissors icon sits on the bottom dotted line where rail meets main area. The main area carries one four-line statement in medium grotesk at 3vw, flush left and flush top, ending in the first quarter of the height. The remaining three quarters are empty.
references.type: Inter Medium at 43px with -0.05em tracking is used once, for the opening statement. Everything else (nav, card copy, counters, FAQ) is Red Hat Mono at 12 to 19px, centred in cards, with braces and italic underlines as state marks.
references.colour: #cdc8c2 #000000 #f8f6f3 #dfe296 — Flat warm grey ground with black ink throughout. Cards alternate off-white and a pale acid yellow-green, the only colour, which appears solely as a card fill.
references.imagery: Loose black brush-and-ink cartoons of anthropomorphic calendars, charts and buildings, scratchy and energetic, each placed alone in the centre of a pale yellow-green near-square card with large rounded corners.
references.layout: A dotted-outline rail stays pinned in the left quarter for the whole page; content scrolls in the remaining three quarters as a two-column grid of near-square cards with 8px gaps, then becomes a single mono list for FAQ. Section titles are only tiny mono labels.

sections.description: Scroll transition after the hero. The single dotted frame splits along a new vertical dotted line at the rail edge as the scissors travel up it; the right-hand piece of the sheet then rotates a few degrees and drops out of view, leaving the rail as its own dotted rectangle. The rail stays pinned while the first row of cards rises from the bottom edge into the vacated area.

Two-column checkerboard of near-square cards about 510px wide with 24px corner radius and 8px gutters. An off-white card holds three centred lines of 13px mono copy with a small '1 of 3' counter beneath; its neighbour is a yellow-green card with one ink cartoon. The next row flips the order, so text and drawing swap sides all the way down. No icons, titles or buttons inside cards.

FAQ as a plain mono list across the right three quarters: a tiny centred label, then questions at 14px, each preceded by a small hollow circle with about 35px between rows. The open item gets a filled dot, an italic underlined question and an indented three-line answer. No dividers, boxes or chevrons; the same hollow and filled circles mark the active item in the rail.

steal: Give the page a physical metaphor that also does layout work: a dotted cut line frames the viewport, then separates the nav rail on scroll.
Alternate text-only and illustration-only cards in a checkerboard, flipping sides each row, instead of packing icon, title and copy into every card.
Use hollow and filled circles as the only state marker for both navigation and accordion items.

references.name: Mosby’s Files
references.idea: An archive of architects presented as a physical stack of coloured index-tab file folders that you flip through.
references.hero: Charcoal background. A slim top bar over a hairline holds the condensed wordmark dead centre and one mono link far right. The headline is one centred line of heavy condensed uppercase at 10vw, about 71% of the width, in the upper quarter. Beneath it, a three-line centred serif paragraph in mid-grey, about 42% wide. From 51% down sits a stack of file folders 86% of the viewport wide: each is a flat colour band with one to three trapezoid tabs rising from its top-left edge, each tab a different colour holding a serif name. Mono category labels sit right-aligned. The front red folder is open, running off the bottom.
references.type: Founders Grotesk bold condensed uppercase at 144px for the title and wordmark; Signifier serif at about 22px for the intro and 28px for tab names; IBM Plex Mono 12px for labels and body. Three unrelated faces, each with one job, and a twelve-to-one size jump.
references.colour: #191919 #d71e1e #1e4bd7 #0c7866 #581e70 #ffe927 — Charcoal ground with five flat poster primaries assigned to folders and tabs; each tab deliberately differs from the folder behind it. No tints, gradients or photos; white type except black on yellow.
references.imagery: No photographs on the index. The folder shapes are the imagery, plus a row of seven small white line-drawn north-arrow and compass symbols and a drawing scale bar borrowed from architectural plans.
references.layout: Centred title block over an 86%-wide folder stack with equal dark margins. Folders overlap at a fixed 60px step so only the tab rows show; the open folder expands into a tall single-colour panel with mono text top-left and plan symbols near the bottom. Under two screens.

sections.description: Four full-width colour bands stacked with a 60px reveal, each with trapezoid tabs growing from its top-left edge. Tabs are about 44px tall with S-curved shoulders, sit side by side with small gaps, and each takes a contrasting flat colour: yellow and black tabs on a green folder, red and blue on purple. Names are white serif at 28px inside the tabs. A mono category label with a small chevron is right-aligned in each band's visible strip.

The front folder opens into a solid red panel nearly two viewports tall. Top-right: its mono category label with a down chevron. Top-left, inset about 60px: a four-line mono paragraph in white, at most half the panel wide. The middle is left empty. Near the bottom, a centred row of seven small white plan symbols evenly spaced; beneath, a baseline row with a drawing scale bar left, year centre, credit and round logo right.

steal: Build navigation as stacked full-width colour bands with trapezoid tabs, each tab coloured to clash with the folder behind it.
Pair a heavy condensed grotesk title with a bookish serif for names and a mono for metadata, giving each face exactly one role.
Borrow notation from the subject's own documents (scale bars, north arrows) as footer ornament instead of generic icons.

references.name: PROOOOF
references.idea: The product's output is the page: a wall of photos each wearing its coloured EXIF strip, with all the copy folded into one small floating card.
references.hero: The whole viewport is a six-column masonry of photographs on a warm off-white ground with about 15px gutters, columns offset vertically so rows never line up. Each photo has a flat strip fused to its bottom edge carrying tiny monospaced capture data, every strip a different solid colour (black, red, orange, yellow, violet, green). Dead centre floats a white card about 380px wide and 410px tall with roughly 28px corner radius and a soft shadow. It contains an extended wordmark with chained O's, a two-row accordion with the first row open, an App Store badge and a monospaced line of links. There is no navigation.
references.type: An extended, heavy wordmark with interlocked O's is the only display type. Card text is Wintyr VF at about 14-16px, medium weight for accordion headings. EXIF strips and footer links are monospace at roughly 8-13px. No headline anywhere.
references.colour: #f3eee9 #fafafa #191818 #ff6a2b #f7c531 #5a4fcf — Colour comes from the photographs and the saturated caption strips, one hue per photo. Card and gutters stay off-white; a final panel flips to near-black with grey characters.
references.imagery: Casual travel, food, pet and concert photos in mixed portrait and landscape crops, square corners, ungraded, tiled edge to edge. The page ends on an ASCII-art rendering of a hand holding a camera.
references.layout: Effectively a single screen: the photo wall sits behind a centred card that carries every word. Six columns on desktop, two on mobile where the card widens to nearly full width. The only second scene is a dark, inset ASCII panel.

sections.description: All product copy lives in the centred card as an accordion: a row with heading left and chevron right, a hairline divider, the open panel's four-line paragraph, a centred store badge, another divider, a collapsed second row, then a small monospaced line with a version number and underlined links. The card stays put while the wall remains visible on all four sides.

Each tile is a photo with a data strip attached below: two or three rows of monospaced text, four values spread evenly across the first row, date and time at opposite ends of the second, maker and model on the third. Strip and text colours change per tile, for example yellow on black, black on yellow, white on violet, so a uniform grid looks varied.

The closing panel is a near-black rectangle inset with wide margins and filled edge to edge with rows of grey ASCII characters that resolve into a picture of a hand gripping a camera. One line of tiny monospaced uppercase text sits at the exact centre as the call to action. No button and no logo.

steal: Show the product's output at wall scale as the background and confine all copy to one small card on top of it.
Give every repeated tile its own flat accent colour for the caption strip so a strict grid reads as lively.
Hold the explanatory copy in an accordion inside the hero card so the page needs no scrolling.
